haiku-low.q1: Postgres stores only the SHA-256 hash. Plaintext appears only in server memory during create, the 201 body, and the browser dialog until closed.
haiku-low.q2: It cannot. The token is shown once when created, and closing the dialog means nobody can show it again.
haiku-low.q3: The 11th create is refused with 409 and a message to revoke a token first. Nothing is written.
haiku-low.q4: On the next API call after the revoke commits, it gets 401, because the lookup reads revoked_at from the primary with no cache.
haiku-low.q5: Unknown, revoked and expired tokens all get 401 with the same generic body and WWW-Authenticate header. The responses do not differ.
haiku-low.q6: The server SHA-256 hashes the token and looks up token_hash on the primary, with no cache. The row is usable only if it exists, is not revoked, and is not expired.
haiku-low.q7: Each successful bearer call records the token id and time in memory, and a batched flush every 5 minutes writes it. No once-per-hour write limit is stated.
haiku-low.q8: The document does not say the request fails. The flush failure is logged, the times are merged back into memory, and the write is retried next interval.
haiku-low.q9: Revoking sets revoked_at on the row, which stays in the table for audit. The row leaves the list, since only active tokens appear.
haiku-low.q10: Another user's or unknown id returns 404 with no change. The user's own already-revoked token returns 204 with no change.
haiku-low.q11: An active row remains that counts toward the 10-token limit, and the token cannot be recovered. The user sees it in the list by name and can revoke it.

sonnet.q1: It stores the SHA-256 hash of the token (token_hash). Plaintext exists only in server memory during the create request, the 201 response body, and the browser dialog memory. Never in DB, logs or analytics.
sonnet.q2: They can't. It is shown once and is unrecoverable. They must revoke it and create a new one.
sonnet.q3: The server rolls back and returns 409 limit reached, with a message to revoke a token first. Nothing is written.
sonnet.q4: On the very next API call after the revoke commits. The lookup reads revoked_at from the primary with no cache, so the first request after the commit gets 401.
sonnet.q5: 401 with the same generic body and the same WWW-Authenticate header in every case. They do not differ.
sonnet.q6: It SHA-256 hashes the token and looks up the row by token_hash on the primary, with no cache. The record is usable if it exists and is active, meaning revoked_at is null and expires_at has not passed (checked on each call).
sonnet.q7: Each successful (active token) API call records the token id and current time in an in-memory map, keeping the latest time per token. A batched flush every 5 minutes writes to the DB. The document does not say a per-token-per-hour write limit exists. NOT STATED for any 'one write per token per hour' mechanism. It only says last-used may be up to 1 hour stale, and the flush is every 5 minutes.
sonnet.q8: NOT STATED for the request itself. The doc only says a failed flush is logged, the snapshot is merged back into memory and retried next interval. The API request is not affected, as the recording happens in memory before the flush.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at to now on the row. The row stays in the table. The token is no longer active, so it disappears from the list and stops counting toward the limit.
sonnet.q10: Another user's (or unknown) token id gives 404 and nothing changes. The user's own already-revoked token gives 204 and nothing changes.
sonnet.q11: The row is committed and active, but the token is unrecoverable. It counts toward the 10-token limit until revoked or expired. The browser shows status unknown with no automatic retry. The user checks the list, where the token appears by name only, and revokes it to free the slot.
